title: The kings undone by their senses
hook: a handbook for kings says its whole science is victory over the senses
carry: indriya jaya: win your own senses first
tomorrow: crumbs on a pond. who eats first, and who stops them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, reasoned inquiry is the lamp of all learning: Gargi in Janaka's court, and the Arthashastra's lamp. Today, the whole science gets a one-line summary.

A phone buzzes, face down on a nightstand. One buzz, and a whole body turns toward it. A smell from the kitchen does the same, or a song from a passing car. The Arthashastra, a handbook for kings, names that pull early on. Then it makes a claim that sounds out of place in a book about armies and treasuries. This whole science, it says, is victory over the senses.
screen: `ONE BUZZ, AND THE BODY TURNS.` → `A BOOK ABOUT ARMIES…` → `…SAYS IT'S ALL ABOUT THE SENSES.`

segments.voice: The phrase is indriya jaya, victory over the senses. The text says what it means: the ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue and the nose don't run wild after sound, touch, sight, taste and smell. Not shut down. Steered. Then it names what has to be given up, and calls them a band of six enemies: desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance and reckless glee. Hindu teachers still warn of six inner enemies, in a slightly different list. A ruler who can't master them, the book warns, soon perishes, even if he holds the whole earth. Then, instead of a lecture, it tells on kings. Dandakya, of the Bhoja line, went after a brahmin's daughter, and was destroyed with his kingdom. Ravana, out of pride, would not give back another man's wife, and lost Lanka and his life. Duryodhana would not give his cousins their share, not even five villages, and got Kurukshetra. The logic is plain. A ruler who can't govern his anger will govern a kingdom with it. So the first territory a king has to win is the five doors of his own body. The throne makes bigger whatever sits on it.
screen: `INDRIYA JAYA: VICTORY OVER THE SENSES.` · `NOT SHUT DOWN. STEERED.` · `SIX INNER ENEMIES.` · `RAVANA, DURYODHANA: ONE PULL EACH.` · then, large: `THE FIRST TERRITORY IS YOU.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus train the senses with japa: one name of God, or a short mantra, repeated slowly, often on a mala of beads. If you pray, choose one name and repeat it softly for the sit. If you don't, pick one sound around you and follow only that. Either way, when something pulls at you, notice the pull, don't chase it, and come back.
The Arthashastra's opening: indriya jaya, victory over the senses, which the book calls the whole of its science.
Hold onto this: indriya jaya, win your own senses first. Ravana couldn't. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1586 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CRUMBS ON A POND. WHO EATS FIRST?`

howItsDone: Hindu teaching on self-mastery speaks of indriya jaya and of six inner enemies, and many Hindus practice it through japa and fasting; in the Arthashastra it is part of a prince's training in its first book, before any word on governing.

myth: conquering the senses means shutting them off completely
the text describes the senses not running wild: steered, not destroyed.
the Arthashastra uses Ravana and Duryodhana as warnings
Ravana's pride and Duryodhana's refusal to share sit in its list of kings undone, next to Dandakya.
a big enough kingdom keeps an unmastered ruler safe

fork.setup: you've just been made captain of your team. in week one, a teammate mouths off at you in front of everyone. by this chapter, what's your first move?
options: bench them on the spot, so everyone sees who's in charge.
notice the anger rising, and let it settle before you decide anything.
ignore it for good; a real captain never lets anything bother them.
fork.reveal: the Arthashastra puts the ruler's own anger first on the list of what to master. it doesn't say nothing should bother you; it says don't let the pull do the ruling.

original.note: Sanskrit indriyajaya, victory over the senses: the theme of Arthashastra 1.6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a book for kings would start with armies.
what it means: it says its whole science is victory over the senses, and it lists kings ruined by one pull each.

what a scholar hears: Arthashastra 1.6, on casting off the arishadvarga, the six enemies (kama, krodha, lobha, mana, mada, harsha), with Dandakya, Ravana and Duryodhana among its examples; later teachers list the six inner enemies a little differently.
recall: reasoned inquiry, the lamp of all sciences
a bow before the first word

chat.says: someone made a MEME of my campaign photo 💀 it's 1am and i'm drafting a clapback. thoughts
options: sleep on it. indriya jaya: the first win is over your own anger.
post it now. a leader who doesn't hit back right away just looks weak.
delete every app. a real leader shuts out everything and feels nothing.
chat.meaning: The Arthashastra calls its whole science indriya jaya, victory over the senses: anger is one of six inner enemies, steered rather than obeyed, and Ravana's pride shows what happens when it rules.

tie.story: Ravana's pride would not let him give Sita back, and the Arthashastra lists him among kings undone by one unmastered pull.
tie.friend: Priya can let the 1am anger settle before she answers the meme, ruling herself before she rules anything else.
tie.you: which pull runs you late at night?

arishadvarga.meaning: the band of six enemies to be cast off

japa.meaning: repeating a name of God or a mantra, often on beads

Dandakya.meaning: a Bhoja king the text says was ruined by desire

Ravana.meaning: the demon king of Lanka in the Ramayana

Duryodhana.meaning: the eldest Kaurava prince in the Mahabharata

sources.ref: Arthashastra 1.6 (control of the senses: ear, skin, eye, tongue and nose with sound, touch, form, taste and smell; the whole science is the conquest of the senses; the six to give up; Dandakya, Ravana, Duryodhana among the kings undone)
Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (the Pandavas' request for five villages, refused by Duryodhana)

notes: Arthashastra run, day 3. Merges the older drafts of 1586 and 1589, which both taught 1.6; vinaya and the elders (1.5) now sit on 1589.

Confirm in Arthashastra 1.6: the definition of control of the senses (ear, skin, eyes, tongue and nose with sound, touch, form, taste and smell); 'this whole science is the conquest of the senses' (1.6.3); the six (kama, krodha, lobha, mana, mada, harsha; rendered desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance, reckless glee) are listed but not counted in the voice; a king without control soon perishes though he hold the whole earth; Dandakya of the Bhoja line; Ravana (would not return another's wife) and Duryodhana (would not part with a portion of the kingdom), both under pride in common editions.
'The five doors of his own body' counts the five senses the text itself names.
Dandakya's gloss has no Devanagari on purpose (spelling not certain).
